steps:
Rule inferred from the 2023->2024 step:
(1) Tier A is the only independently indexed value: A_year = 100,000 x cumulative CPI-U factor (2023 factor 1.24331, 2024 factor 1.30461).
(2) Tiers B/C/D are NOT independently inflated -- each year they are recomputed as 3% / 20% / 1% of the NEW tier A.
(3) Every published value is rounded to whole dollars; round-to-nearest is confirmed by B (3,913.83 -> 3,914) and D (1,304.61 -> 1,305). Tier C's two observations both have fractional part .20 (24,866.20 and 26,092.20), so round-nearest and truncate are indistinguishable there; I use round-nearest and flag it -- the two rules agree whenever the fraction is under 0.50.
Why this rule rather than inflating each tier: the B/C/D ratios to A are exactly 3.000%/20.000%/1.000% in both years, which cannot happen if four independently rounded series were inflated separately.

steps:
Candidate mechanisms sized against the observed 56 / 4.27 bp miss:
(a) Whole-dollar rounding convention: bounded at +/-0.50 per tier, i.e. <=0.04 bp on a 134k base. Observed miss is 56. RULED OUT -- too small by ~110x.
(b) Tier-C truncate vs round-nearest ambiguity: bounded at 1 and only affects tier C. RULED OUT for the tier A miss.
(c) Published-percentage precision: '3.4%' is a one-decimal rounding of the true CPI-U increase. A +/-5 bp error in a rate applied to 130,461 is +/-65. Observed miss 56 sits inside this band. MATCHES in both sign and magnitude, and the identical signature appears in the 2023->2024 step (stated 4.9%, actual 4.9304%, naive-1.049 error $38 on tier A).
(d) Index vintage / which 12-month CPI-U window is used: could shift the rate by tens of bp, so it is a real risk, but it cannot be the discriminator here because the stated 3.4% already rounds consistently to the official value -- no vintage change is needed to explain the data.
Strongest single mechanism: (c).
answer: The published 3.4% is a CPI-U increase rounded to one decimal; the official dollar figures are computed from the unrounded index ratio (2024 actual 1.0493039 = 4.9304%, 2025 actual 1.0335733 = 3.3573%). Applying a rate rounded to the nearest 10 bp against a ~130,461 base injects up to +/-65 of error -- about 110x the +/-0.50 whole-dollar rounding error, which is the only other mechanism in play. That is precisely the size and direction of the observed miss (56 low = 4.27 bp). Remedy: never use the published rounded percentage; recompute factor = CPI-U(index month, year N) / CPI-U(index month, year N-1) at full precision and apply it to the cumulative base.

weakest_point: The 3.4% input is itself a rounded number -- a CPI-U increase published to one decimal -- while the official 2025 tier A was produced from the unrounded index ratio 1.0335733 (3.3573%). My projection inherits that rounding: a rate rounded to the nearest 10 bp, applied to a 130,461 base, moves the answer by up to about 65, and the observed miss is 56 low (4.27 bp). The corroborating signature is that the 2023->2024 step behaves identically (stated 4.9%, actual 4.9304%, naive-1.049 error 38 on tier A), so this is a systematic feature of using the headline percentage rather than the index ratio -- not a one-off. Whole-dollar rounding convention is bounded at +/-$0.50 and cannot explain any of it.
